query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, dynamic recrystallization and concomitant precipitation (e.g., formation of M23C6 carbides or Cr-rich σ phase) at grain boundaries in the eutectic high-entropy alloy create microstructural discontinuities that both concentrate local stresses and disrupt the integrity of protective oxide/passive films. These effects synergistically accelerate degradation by enhancing wear (via localized micro-cracking and material removal) and corrosion (through the loss of passivation and initiation of pitting).
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with a balanced matrix containing stable second-phase particles under standard processing conditions.
generation.intervention: Exposure to simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosive environments at elevated temperatures (approximately 500–600 °C).
generation.conditions: Tests conducted at high temperature (500–600 °C) under a controlled, simultaneous wear-corrosion environment (constant mechanical sliding combined with a corrosive media with defined pH and ionic strength).
generation.structural_mediator: Dynamic precipitates forming along grain boundaries during stress-assisted recrystallization.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperature accelerates dynamic recrystallization and precipitation, which increase local heterogeneities. The precipitates act as both mechanical barriers and corrosion initiation sites by disrupting continuous passive films and concentrating stress, leading to synergistic degradation through both wear (enhanced micro-cracking and material removal) and corrosion (accelerated pitting and film breakdown).
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline alloy with a more stable microstructure (achieved by processing that minimizes dynamic recrystallization/precipitation), the test alloy will show an increase in overall degradation. Specifically, there will be a higher wear rate due to increased micro-cracking at grain boundaries and a faster corrosion rate, as pitting and passivation failure become more pronounced at the precipitate sites.
generation.baseline: A matched alloy of similar composition processed (e.g., via rapid quenching or lower-temperature annealing) to suppress dynamic recrystallization and precipitation, thereby maintaining a more continuous passive layer under the same environmental conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds under conditions where the temperature is sufficiently high (around 500–600 °C) to induce dynamic microstructural evolution, and where simultaneous mechanical wear and a consistent corrosive environment (with controlled pH and ionic content) are maintained.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contributions of the increased wear vs. the enhanced corrosion to the overall degradation, as well as the sensitivity of these effects to variations in precipitate size, distribution, and phase nature, are uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of multi-phase eutectic HEA samples: one set processed to allow significant dynamic recrystallization and precipitation (via slower cooling/higher-temperature exposure) and a control set processed to suppress these microstructural changes (via rapid quenching or lower-temperature treatment). Subject both sets to identical elevated temperature (500–600 °C) conditions under simultaneous mechanical wear and controlled corrosion (with fixed pH and ionic composition).
measurements: Wear rate (surface micro-cracking and material removal)
Corrosion rate (pitting density and breakdown of passive films)
Microstructural characterization (using SEM/TEM to evaluate grain boundary precipitates and recrystallized zones)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with enhanced dynamic recrystallization/precipitation do not display significantly higher total degradation—specifically, higher wear and corrosion rates compared to the control set with a stable microstructure—then the hypothesis that dynamic precipitate formation coupled with recrystallization accelerates the degradation is falsified.

Question: What are the creep deformation mechanisms and microstructural evolution characteristics of an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy in the intermediate temperature range of 500–600 °C?. System: Equiatomic Co20Cr20Fe20Ni20Mn20 (atomic percentage) FCC-structured high-entropy alloy. Processing: Vacuum induction melting with 99.9 mass% purity elements, re-melted five times, drop-cast, homogenized at 1100 °C for 24 h, cold-rolled 40%, and annealed at 900 °C for 1 h. Test conditions: Tensile creep tests at 500, 550, and 600 °C under applied stresses of 140–400 MPa; interrupted tests at steady-state stages cooled with liquid nitrogen.
